passage:
Counsellor's note, Tanvir. Zainab, fifteen, came in after her mother phoned the school about her "shutting herself in." Zainab said she keeps her door closed to write and think, and that last week she found her mother reading her diary and checking her phone. She feels "watched, like a suspect," and now answers in single words at home.
Nothing she described points to danger; she talks about friends and her writing. I will meet her mother tomorrow, share only what Zainab agrees to, and suggest a knock, a cup of tea and being around instead of questions. If Zainab's mood or routine changes, I will follow up at once.

qa.q: What did Zainab's mother read last week?
qa.a: Her diary, and she also checked Zainab's phone.

qa.q: How does Zainab feel about her mother's checking?
qa.a: Watched and distrusted, 'like a suspect', so she now answers in single words at home.

qa.q: What could Zainab's mother do instead of checking, according to Tanvir?
qa.a: Knock, offer a cup of tea and be around, instead of asking questions or reading the diary.

qa.q: How might Zainab's mother feel about the closed door?
qa.a: Probably worried, since she phoned the school about it, and afraid of missing something.

grounding: A teenager who shuts the door wants privacy, and respecting it while staying available preserves trust.

passage:
Tuesday night. Something good happened today. When I came home I went straight to my room and shut the door. A month ago Amma would have knocked five times and asked, "What happened? Tell me!" Today she knocked once and said, "Tea's on the table when you want it. I'm in the kitchen." Then nothing.
My little brother Yash tried to peek through the keyhole, and Amma called him away: "Let her be."
I sat on my bed and wrote a poem nobody will read. By seven I was hungry and chatty, so I came out on my own and told Amma about the maths test before she asked. Maybe privacy isn't the opposite of closeness.
Sudha

qa.q: Who tried to peek through the keyhole?
qa.a: Yash, Sudha's little brother.

qa.q: What is Sudha feeling about how Amma handled the closed door?
qa.a: Sudha feels relieved and trusted, and pleased enough to come out and share the news about the maths test.

qa.q: What choice by Amma made the evening go differently from a month ago?
qa.a: Amma knocked once, offered tea, said she was in the kitchen and did not ask questions.

qa.q: How might Yash see the closed door?
qa.a: Yash seems curious and wants to peek, until Amma calls him away.

grounding: A teenager wants a closed door and no questions, and is respected while a parent stays quietly available.

passage:
"Chinmay, I'm going to the market. Want anything?"
"No." The door stayed shut.
Sachin paused outside it. That morning his wife had asked him to find out what was going on with their son. He could hear music, low.
"Okay. I'll be back by seven. If you want to talk about anything, I'm around tonight. No questions otherwise."
Silence. Then: "Papa?"
"Yes?"
"Can you get the good biscuits?"
Sachin smiled at the door. "The good biscuits. Done."
That night after dinner, Chinmay came and sat next to him on the balcony. He didn't say much. He talked a little about a song he was writing. Sachin just listened.

qa.q: What did Chinmay ask his father to buy?
qa.a: The good biscuits.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay have come to sit on the balcony later?
qa.a: He likely felt trusted and safe, since his father respected the closed door and said he was around without pushing questions.

qa.q: What did Sachin do instead of finding out what was going on?
qa.a: He respected the closed door, said when he'd be back and that he was around, with no questions otherwise.

qa.q: What would change if Sachin had demanded to know what Chinmay was doing?
qa.a: Chinmay might have shut down further and never mentioned the song he was writing.

grounding: Shows a teenager's need for a closed door respected by a parent who stays quietly available, keeping trust.

passage:
When I was fifteen, I kept a notebook of poems under my mattress. Nobody knew about it. One afternoon I came home and found it on my bed, open. My older sister Kashish had read it and was laughing about one line with her friend on the phone.
I didn't speak to her for a week. I started locking my door, answering everything with "nothing", writing only in my head.
Months later Kashish came to my door and knocked instead of walking in. "I'm sorry about the poems. I won't touch your things again. If you ever want me to read one, I'd like that. If not, that's fine." Then she left. It took a while, but a year later I showed her one. I'm Tanuja, and I still knock on her door too.

qa.q: Where did Tanuja keep the notebook of poems?
qa.a: Under the mattress.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel on finding the notebook open?
qa.a: Tanuja felt hurt and betrayed, and stopped speaking to Kashish for a week.

qa.q: What did Kashish's apology get right?
qa.a: She knocked, apologised, promised not to touch Tanuja's things, and left the choice to share with Tanuja.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt when Tanuja finally showed a poem?
qa.a: Kashish likely felt touched and grateful that trust had come back.

grounding: Shows a teenager's private inner life invaded, and trust rebuilt when the sibling respects privacy and stays available.

passage:
Boarding house note, girls' wing, Sunday.
Trisha, 15, has started spending Sunday afternoons alone in the music room with the door closed. Two staff members asked me to check what she's up to. I don't think surveillance is the answer.
I knocked once today and said, "Just letting you know I'm in the office till five if you need anything." She said, "Thanks, Ganga Ma'am," and the door stayed shut. I didn't open it.
At five she came to the office on her own and asked if she could use the music room every Sunday. She is teaching herself the keyboard and didn't want anyone listening while she's still bad at it.
Next step: I've booked the room for her on Sundays, 2 to 5.
Ganga

qa.q: What is Trisha teaching herself?
qa.a: The keyboard.

qa.q: Why did Trisha want the door closed?
qa.a: She felt shy and self-conscious, not wanting anyone to hear while she's still bad at the keyboard.

qa.q: What did Ganga do instead of checking on her?
qa.a: Ganga knocked once, said where to find help, didn't open the door, and later booked the room for Trisha.

qa.q: What would change if the staff had checked what Trisha was up to?
qa.a: Trisha might have felt watched and stopped practising or hidden it, instead of asking openly for the room.

grounding: Shows a teenager's wish for privacy respected by an adult who stays available, so she comes forward herself.

passage:
Friday night
Came home from school and shut my door. Didn't want anyone. I'm writing my own songs now, in this notebook, and they're mine, not for anyone to read yet.
Mummy knocked once. I thought, here we go: "What are you doing? Who are you talking to? Open the door." Bua does that to my cousin, reads her messages and everything.
But Mummy just said through the door, "Tenzin, there's momos in the kitchen. I'll be on the balcony if you want company." Then she went away.
I stayed in my room another hour and finished the second verse. Then I went out to the balcony and sat with her. We didn't talk much. At some point I told her I was writing songs. She said, "I'd love to hear one someday. Only when you want."
Kalyani Tamang, my mummy, is the best.

qa.q: What is Tenzin writing in the notebook?
qa.a: Tenzin is writing songs in the notebook.

qa.q: What did Tenzin expect when Mummy knocked?
qa.a: Tenzin felt wary and defensive, expecting questions and pressure to open the door, like Bua does with the cousin.

qa.q: Why did Mummy's approach build trust?
qa.a: She respected the closed door, offered food and her company without conditions, and didn't demand to hear the songs.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have felt sitting on the balcony that evening?
qa.a: Kalyani likely felt patient and quietly hopeful, and touched when Tenzin came out and shared about the songs.

grounding: A teenager who shuts the door is building an inner life, and a parent who respects solitude while staying available keeps trust.
